title: The Alphabet, Sounds, and Stress
summary: The thirty-two letters, the distinction between short and long vowels, the softening i, the diphthongs, and why Lithuanian stress must be learned word by word.

notes: The letters q, w and x do not belong to the alphabet. They appear only in untranslated foreign names.

Alphabetical order places each diacritical letter immediately after its plain counterpart: a, ą, b, c, č, … i, į, y, … u, ų, ū, v, z, ž. Note that y follows į, not i, and is filed among the i-letters rather than at the end.

rules.heading: The Alphabet
rules.statement: The Lithuanian alphabet has **thirty-two** letters. It is the Latin alphabet with **q**, **w** and **x** removed, and nine letters added by means of three diacritical marks: the *nosinė* or hook (**ą ę į ų**), the *paukščiukas* or háček (**č š ž**), and the length marks on **ė** and **ū**. A tenth addition, **y**, is written without a diacritic but is nonetheless a distinct letter.
footnotes: The diacritics are not optional ornaments. Dropping the hook from ą or the bar from ū changes the word, and often the grammar: kąsti, to bite, is not kasti, to dig.

rules.heading: Short and Long Vowels
rules.statement: Every Lithuanian vowel is either **short** or **long**, and the difference distinguishes words. Some letters are fixed in length and some are not: **ė, ū, į, y, ų, ą, ę** are always long, **i** and **u** are always short, and **a, e, o** vary — short when unstressed, long when stressed (**o** being long in all native words). It follows that the spelling alone tells you the length of most vowels, but not of a, e and o.

examples.note: long ū — a different word entirely

rules.heading: The Nosinė Letters
rules.statement: The four letters **ą, ę, į, ų** carry a hook called the *nosinė*, "the nasal one". They once marked a nasalised vowel, as the name records; in the modern language the nasality is gone and they are simply **long vowels**. The hook is retained because it marks grammatical endings — the accusative singular of nouns ends in a nosinė vowel — and because it distinguishes otherwise identical words.

examples.note: the hook is the whole of the accusative ending
the same letters without the hook

footnotes: Because the nosinė is a long vowel and nothing more, ų and ū sound alike, as do į and y. Which is written is fixed by grammar and etymology, not by sound.

rules.heading: Consonants Differing from English
rules.statement: Most consonants have their expected values. Six require attention: **c** is always /ts/, never /k/ or /s/; **č** is *ch* as in "church"; **š** is *sh*; **ž** is the *s* of "measure"; **j** is the *y* of "yes", never the *j* of "jam"; and **r** is trilled with the tip of the tongue. **p, t, k** are unaspirated: they lack the puff of breath that follows them in English "pin, tin, kin".

rules.heading: The Consonant Digraphs Ch, Dz, Dž
rules.statement: Three pairs of letters stand for **single consonants**: **ch** is /x/, the *ch* of Scottish "loch"; **dz** is /dz/, the voiced counterpart of c; and **dž** is /dʒ/, the *j* of "jam". They are not separate letters of the alphabet and are alphabetised as the two letters they are written with.

rules.heading: The Softening I
rules.statement: Before the back vowels **a, ą, o, u, ų, ū** an **i** is written that is **not pronounced as a vowel**. Its office is to mark the preceding consonant as *soft* (palatalised), the consonant being pronounced with the tongue raised towards the palate, much as in English "onion" or "million". Reading such an i as a full vowel is the commonest mistake a beginner makes.

examples.note: the i softens š; the vowel is the diphthong au
the i softens ž; the vowel is e

footnotes: Before the front vowels e, ė, ę, i, į, y a consonant is soft automatically, and no i is written.

rules.heading: Diphthongs
rules.statement: Two vowels written together in one syllable form a **diphthong**, pronounced as a single glide. The native diphthongs are **ai, au, ei, ie, ui, uo**; **oi** and **eu** occur chiefly in loanwords. Of these, **ie** and **uo** are peculiar to Lithuanian: they begin at the first vowel and glide towards a central sound, and they are never a sequence of two separate vowels.

rules.heading: Spelling and Pronunciation
rules.statement: Lithuanian spelling is very nearly phonemic: every letter written is pronounced, no letter is silent, and one letter stands for one sound. The exceptions are the softening **i** of ¶6, the three digraphs of ¶5, and the assimilation of voice in consonant clusters, whereby a consonant takes the voicing of the one following it.

examples.note: pronounced *dirpti*: b takes the voicelessness of t

rules.heading: Stress
rules.statement: Stress in Lithuanian is **free** — it may fall on any syllable of a word — and **mobile** — it may move from one syllable to another as the word is inflected. It is therefore not predictable from the spelling and must be learned with each word. In ordinary writing it is **not marked at all**; the accent marks are used only in dictionaries, grammars and schoolbooks. This course marks stress in vocabulary lists and omits it in reading passages, as printed Lithuanian does.

examples.note: the stress moves to the ending in the plural

footnotes: Three marks are used when stress is shown: the grave ` on short stressed vowels, and the acute ´ and tilde ˜ on long ones, which distinguish two tones. Tone is taken up at C1; for now, note only the position of the stress.

vocabulary.notes: Pronounced AH-choo: the i softens č and is not a vowel.

drills.stem: How many letters are there in the Lithuanian alphabet?
drills.explanation: Thirty-two: Latin without q, w, x, plus ą ę į ų, č š ž, ė ū and y (¶1). Tempting 26 counts only the English alphabet; 29 forgets the three háček letters or the nosinė set.

drills.stem: Which letter does **not** belong to the Lithuanian alphabet?
drills.explanation: q, w and x were left out and appear only in untranslated foreign names (¶1). ų, š and ė are all native letters formed with diacritics.

drills.stem: The letter **ę** is pronounced:
options: as a short e, like English 'bet'
as a long close vowel, like French 'été'
as a long broad vowel, like a drawn-out 'bad'
identically to ė in every position
drills.explanation: ę is always the long broad /æː/. The close long vowel is ė; short e is plain e; ę and ė are different letters and different sounds (¶2–¶3).

drills.stem: Which letters represent a **long** vowel in every word they occur in?
drills.explanation: ą and ū are fixed long (¶2–¶3). i is always short; a is variable — long only when stressed. Choosing a is the classic trap of confusing "can be long" with "always long".

drills.stem: *butas* "apartment" vs *būtas* "been". What alone distinguishes them in speech?
options: the length of the vowel written u / ū
drills.explanation: u is always short and ū always long (¶2). Length alone separates the words; stress position and soft-i are red herrings here.

drills.stem: In *ačiū* ("thank you"), what is the letter **i** doing?
options: It forms a diphthong iu with ū.
It softens č and is not itself a pronounced vowel.
It is a separate syllable: a-či-ū.
It is silent historical spelling with no phonetic effect.
drills.explanation: Before a back vowel, written i only marks soft č; the word has two syllables, AH-choo (¶6). Reading i as a full vowel (three syllables) is the beginner's most common soft-i error.

drills.stem: Which of the following are **diphthongs** (two vowel letters as one glide)?
drills.explanation: uo and ie are native diphthongs (¶7). ch and dž are digraphs for single consonants (¶5) — near-miss if you confuse "two letters" with "two vowels".

drills.stem: The letter **c** in *centas* is pronounced:
drills.explanation: c is invariably /ts/ (¶4). /tʃ/ is č; /s/ and /k/ are English transfer errors.

drills.stem: How many vowel letters are **always long**, regardless of stress?
drills.explanation: Seven: ą, ę, ė, į, y, ų, ū (¶2). Answering 4 counts only the nosinė set; answering 5 adds ė ū but forgets y; answering 9 wrongly includes variable a, e, o.

drills.stem: Which statements about the letter **y** are correct?
options: It is pronounced identically to į.
In alphabetical order it stands immediately after į.
It represents the consonant glide of English 'yes'.
drills.explanation: y is long i, sounding like į, and is filed i, į, y (¶1–¶2). The glide of 'yes' is j (¶4) — the classic English transfer distractor.

drills.stem: In *chemija*, *dzūkas* and *džiaugtis*, how many **digraphs** (two letters for one consonant sound) appear in total?
drills.explanation: Three: *ch* in *chemija*, *dz* in *dzūkas*, *dž* in *džiaugtis*. Each is one sound, not two.

drills.stem: Which statement about Lithuanian stress is correct?
options: It falls on the penultimate syllable, as in Polish.
It is free and mobile, and is not marked in ordinary writing.
It always falls on the first syllable, as in Finnish.
It is marked with an acute accent in all printed texts.
drills.explanation: Stress may fall on any syllable and may shift under inflection (*namas* → *namai*); accent marks belong to dictionaries, not ordinary print (¶9).

drills.stem: Which pairs are **homophones** in modern Lithuanian (same sound, different spelling)?
options: ą and a (when a is unstressed)
drills.explanation: į/y and ų/ū are both simply long /iː/ and /uː/ (¶3 footnote). ę is broad /æː/ while ė is close /eː/; unstressed a is short, never equal to always-long ą (¶2).

drills.stem: Which of the following are **diphthongs**?
drills.explanation: *ai* and *uo* are vowel glides. *ch* and *dž* are consonant digraphs, not diphthongs.

drills.stem: The digraph **ch** is alphabetised as:
options: a separate letter between c and č
the two letters c then h, not a letter of its own
drills.explanation: ch, dz and dž are digraphs for single sounds but are not separate alphabet letters; they are filed as the two letters written (¶5).

drills.stem: Which letter is **always** a long close /eː/?
drills.explanation: *ė* is always the long close 'ay' (¶2). Plain *e* varies with stress; *ę* is the long broad /æː/; *ie* is a diphthong (¶7).

drills.stem: In *žiema* (“winter”), what is **i** doing before **e**?
options: Marking soft ž before a back vowel
Standing as a full vowel syllable
Forming the diphthong ie with e
drills.explanation: *ie* is a native diphthong (¶7). Soft-i (¶6) appears only before back vowels a/ą/o/u/ų/ū — not before *e*.

drills.stem: Which statements about **c / č / š / ž** are correct?
options: ž is pronounced like English *z* in *zoo*
drills.explanation: ¶4: c=/ts/, č=church, š=sh, ž=measure (not English *zoo* /z/).

drills.stem: *kąsti* “to bite” vs *kasti* “to dig”. What alone distinguishes them in **spelling**?
drills.explanation: The nosinė *ą* marks the always-long vowel historically nasal; modern speech may sound similar, but spelling keeps the hook (¶3).

drills.stem: Which statements about Lithuanian spelling are **correct**?
options: Almost every letter written is pronounced
Silent letters are common as in English
Softening i is an exception that is written but not a vowel nucleus
Digraphs ch, dz, dž count as one sound each
drills.explanation: Spelling is nearly phonemic: almost every letter is sounded. Softening *i* is written but not a vowel nucleus; *ch, dz, dž* are one sound each. English-style silent letters are not the rule.

drills.stem: How many letters does the Lithuanian alphabet contain that are **not** in the basic Latin set of twenty-six?
drills.explanation: ¶1 adds nine letters with diacritics: ą ę į ų, č š ž, ė ū (y already exists in Latin). Tempting 6 forgets ė/ū/y-count mistakes; 3 counts only háčeks.

drills.stem: Alphabetising **chemija**: where does **ch** sort relative to **c** and **č**?
options: As its own letter after h
Under c, as the digraph beginning with c
Under č, because it sounds similar
At the end of the alphabet
drills.explanation: ¶5: digraphs are not separate alphabet letters; *ch* is filed under *c*.

drills.stem: Which words contain a **softening i** (not a vowel nucleus)?
drills.explanation: *siūlas* and *šiaurė* have i before back vowels ū/a (¶6). *duona* has diphthong *uo*; *lietus* has sequential vowels in separate roles, not soft-i before a back vowel.

drills.stem: Why must stress be learned **word by word**?
options: It always falls on the first syllable
It is free and may also move under inflection
It is identical to Polish fixed stress
drills.explanation: ¶9: free and mobile; ordinary print omits marks, so each lemma’s stress must be learned.

drills.stem: How many of **q, w, x** appear in the Lithuanian alphabet?
drills.explanation: ¶1 removes q, w, x from Latin. Answering 3 confuses “Latin letters known to Lithuanians” with alphabet membership.

drills.stem: The digraph **dz** is:
options: two separate alphabet letters counted in the 32
alphabetised as its own letter after d
drills.explanation: ¶5: dz=/dz/, voiced counterpart of c; digraphs are not separate alphabet letters.

drills.stem: Which letters are **always long** wherever they occur?
drills.explanation: ¶2: ė ū į y ų ą ę are always long; plain *i* is short.

drills.stem: **j** in *labas* is pronounced like:
drills.explanation: ¶4: *j* is the glide /j/ as in *yes*. English *jam* is closer to digraph *dž*.

drills.stem: How many **syllables** are there in *šiaurė*?
drills.explanation: Two: *šiau-rė*. Soft-*i* is not a nucleus, and *au* is a single diphthong. Treating soft-*i* as a vowel wrongly gives three.

drills.stem: Which pair differs **only** by vowel length in speech?
drills.explanation: *butas* (short *u*) vs *būtas* (long *ū*) is the classic length contrast. The others invent contrasts or change consonants.

drills.title: Abėcėlė ir garsai
drills.passage: Lietuvių abėcėlė turi trisdešimt dvi raides. Raidė y yra balsis, ne priebalsis. Žodyje ačiū raidė i minkština č. Žodyje duona yra diftongas uo. Žodyje šiaurė yra minkštinantis i ir diftongas au. Kirtis lietuvių kalboje yra laisvas: jis gali kristi ant bet kurio skiemens.
drills.translation: The Lithuanian alphabet has thirty-two letters. The letter y is a vowel, not a consonant. In the word ačiū the letter i softens č. In the word duona there is the diphthong uo. In the word šiaurė there is a softening i and the diphthong au. Stress in the Lithuanian language is free: it may fall on any syllable.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is **y**?
questions.explanation: The passage states *Raidė y yra balsis, ne priebalsis* — y is a vowel (¶1–¶2). The 'yes' glide is j.

questions.stem: Which claims does the passage make about **šiaurė**?
options: It contains three full vowel syllables from i, a and ė.
The i before au is itself a pronounced vowel.
questions.explanation: The passage names soft-i and diphthong au. Treating i as a full vowel would invent a third syllable the text never asserts (¶6–¶7).

questions.stem: How many syllables does the passage's analysis imply for **ačiū**?
questions.explanation: Soft-i means i is not a vowel nucleus, so ačiū is a-čiū — two syllables (¶6). Answering 3 treats the soft-i as a vowel.

questions.stem: The passage says stress is *laisvas*. What does that mean?
options: Stress always falls on the first syllable.
Stress may fall on any syllable and need not be predictable from spelling.
Stress is printed with an acute in every book.
Stress is fixed once learned for the nominative and never moves.
questions.explanation: Free stress: it may fall on any syllable and is not predictable from ordinary spelling. It is also unmarked in print and may move under inflection.

questions.stem: Which words does the passage explicitly treat as containing a **diphthong**?
questions.explanation: *duona* has uo; *šiaurė* has au. *ačiū* has soft-i + ū, not a diphthong iu; *abėcėlė* has sequential vowels in separate syllables.
